name: Oroko (Ŋgóló)
overview: The Ŋgóló, one of the clans of the Oroko people, live in good harmony with their neighbours and with the migrants from the Grassfields whom they call báŋgárà. Coming from Ísàkà (Bakassi) via Màtùbà, they have a loosely centralised chiefdom and a sacred house, the étánà, which preserves the culture of the village; coffee, food crops, hunting and livestock rearing provide their living.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: The group lives with neighbours and with migrants from the West and North-West, called báŋgárà (“people of the Grassfields”).
The speech variety is close to that of the Batanga of the Océan (South).
Exogamous marriages, for men and women alike; good relations with non-natives.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Land of the ancestors, which belongs to them, with no particular religious significance.
Having come from Ísàkà (now Bakassi) via Màtùbà, they still exchange with these places: they invite one another to the festivals of cultural associations.
The early European presence on the coast weakened the culture and explains a loosely structured chiefdom.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kingship less centralised than in the West, the North-West or the Far North.
The chief decides after discussion with the kingmakers (today also with the elites), with little constraint on those who do not obey.
Non-natives integrated among the kingmakers or married to a ŋgóló girl may buy land; the “village lands” are sold only with everyone's agreement.
No restriction in relationships; only the ordinary rules of respect apply (children greet their elders).
Neighbouring villages are regarded as brothers.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's house.
There is neither a fixed age nor a rite for becoming a man or a woman, nor for marrying: everything depends on maturity.
Steps: learning about the procedure, then customary marriage.
Bride price: palm wine (libation to the ancestors), kola nuts, a sow and a goat (symbols of fertility), crate of beer, money.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The ancestor cult is held at the étánà, a house built in the centre of the village, where blessings are given and where all the culture is kept; guardians live there permanently. In front of it stands the màbádò stone.
Only the birth of twins, children with supernatural powers, has particular significance.
Death takes one back to the ancestors, who are called upon in case of misfortune.
Killing a person, or certain animals considered as persons (dog, cat, goat), angers the ancestors and requires purification.
Non-initiates are forbidden to see the night dance ŋgányià, on pain of illness.
The body of a person who died a violent death is not brought into the village.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Activities: coffee, hunting, food crops, poultry farming, pig farming.
Anyone can buy and own land; the proceeds from the sale of village land go towards the village's development.
Ancestral crafts not intended for sale: woven bags, carved armchairs, to decorate the house.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men wear the sànjà (wrapper tied at the waist) over a multicoloured jumpa shirt, now often replaced by a white long-sleeved shirt; initiates of the étánà add a nyariphu headdress. Women wear the kàbà.
Strong trust in traditional medicine, inherited from the ancestors.
No fixed standard of beauty: above all a hardworking spouse from a family of good reputation is sought.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Àmɛ́kɔ̀kɔ́ to welcome newborns; màlé at the death of a member and during cultural events; ŋgányià at the death of an initiate; ndìsòŋgó for village ceremonies.
Instruments: élìmb' and èsìmbí drums, ŋgájíká horn.
No festival of its own, but end-of-year celebrations organised by the development association.

sections.title: The names
items: No particular structure; the name depends on circumstances.
Names are changed in the negative sense, because it is believed that the name influences life.

lessons.title: Who are the Oroko (Ŋgóló)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Oroko (Ŋgóló) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The group lives with neighbours and with migrants from the West and North-West, called báŋgárà (“people of the Grassfields”). • The speech variety is close to that of the Batanga of the Océan (South). • Exogamous marriages, for men and women alike; good relations with non-natives. • Land of the ancestors, which belongs to them, with no particular religious significance. • Having come from Ísàkà (today Bakassi) via Màtùbà, they still exchange with those places: people invite each other to the festivals of the cultural associations.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ŋgóló, one of the clans of the Oroko people, live in good harmony with their neighbours and with the migrants from the Grassfields whom they call báŋgárà. Coming from Ísàkà (Bakassi) via Màtùbà, they have a loosely centralised chiefdom and a sacred house, the étánà, which preserves the culture of the village; coffee, food crops, hunting and livestock rearing provide their living.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Oroko (Ŋgóló) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Oroko (Ŋgóló)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Oroko (Ŋgóló).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Oroko (Ŋgóló).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: gwáráŋgà and ìtókó (yellow macabo fufu and sauce), bìkɛ́rɛ́ and bɛ́rɛ́mìɛ̀ (plantain and macabo leaves). • Drinks: palm wine. • Activities: coffee, hunting, food crops, poultry farming, pig farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Oroko (Ŋgóló) eat mainly gwáráŋgà and ìtókó, bìkɛ́rɛ́ and bɛ́rɛ́mìɛ̀. Traditional drinks: palm wine. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Oroko (Ŋgóló): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Àmɛ́kɔ̀kɔ́ to welcome newborns; màlé at the death of a member and during cultural events; ŋgányià at the death of an initiate; ndìsòŋgó for village ceremonies. • Instruments: élìmb' and èsìmbí drums, ŋgájíká horn. • No festival of its own, but end-of-year celebrations organised by the development association.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Oroko (Ŋgóló), traditional dances (àmɛ́kɔ̀kɔ́, mourning, cultural events, ŋgányià) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: élìmb' and èsìmbí drums, ŋgájíká horn. Festival(s): the village's end-of-year festivals.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Oroko (Ŋgóló)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Oroko (Ŋgóló). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Oroko (Ŋgóló). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Activities: coffee, hunting, subsistence crops, poultry farming, pig rearing. • Everyone can buy and own land; the proceeds from the sale of the village's land serve its development. • Ancestral crafts not intended for sale: woven bags, carved armchairs, to decorate the house.

lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Oroko (Ŋgóló)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Oroko (Ŋgóló). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Oroko (Ŋgóló), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Oroko (Ŋgóló). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Ancestor worship is held at the étánà, a house built at the centre of the village, where blessings are given and where all the culture is kept; guardians live there permanently. In front of it stands the màbádò stone. • Only the birth of twins, children with supernatural powers, has particular significance. • Death leads back to the ancestors, who are called upon in times of misfortune. • Killing a person, or certain animals regarded as persons (dog, cat, goat), angers the ancestors and requires purification. • The uninitiated are forbidden to see the ŋgányià night dance, on pain of illness.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The ancestor cult is held at the étánà, a house built in the centre of the village, where blessings are given and where all the culture is kept; guardians live there permanently. In front of it stands the màbádò stone. Only the birth of twins, children with supernatural powers, carries particular significance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Oroko (Ŋgóló) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Oroko, ŋgóló dialect
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Oroko (Ŋgóló) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Oroko (Ŋgóló) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Oroko (Ŋgóló) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Oroko (Ŋgóló) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Oroko, ŋgóló dialect. • Greetings: Bútjérî = morning greeting (one person); Bútjérî mì = morning greeting (several people); Wùsájè = midday greeting (one person). • Counting from 1 to 5: Èjɔ́kɔ́, Bê bɛ́, Béràro, Bé né, Bé tá. • Names are changed in the negative sense, because people believe that a name influences life.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Oroko, ŋgóló dialect are the first steps towards communicating with the Oroko (Ŋgóló). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
